items.text: Moral concern is a finite resource that can be misallocated

Attributing or withholding consciousness to AI does not just affect beliefs about machines; it reallocates a limited stock of human ethical attention and care, so getting it wrong distorts how that attention is spent elsewhere.

The claim that mistaken attributions 'distort our ethical priorities' or our 'circles of moral concern' only makes sense if moral concern is treated as a scarce, zero-sum resource rather than something that can simply expand to include more objects at no cost.
Under deep uncertainty about machine minds, caution overrides curiosity

When we cannot be sure whether creating a system would make it a conscious moral patient, the right response is to refrain from creating it rather than to proceed and find out, even though the same uncertainty could in principle justify either course.

The essay moves straight from 'nobody knows for certain' to 'nobody should try' without arguing why uncertainty licenses prohibition rather than permission or neutrality; the reader has to already accept a precautionary stance toward new moral patients for that inference to hold.
Intelligence and consciousness are separate properties

Intelligence is about doing — achieving complex goals by flexible means — while consciousness is about being, about there being something it is like to have an experience at all. A system can have one without the other.
Anthropocentric biases make us over-attribute consciousness

Three linked biases — anthropocentrism, human exceptionalism, and anthropomorphism — lead people to assume that anything showing humanlike behavior, especially language, must also have humanlike inner experience.
Computational functionalism is an unproven assumption

The belief that conscious AI is possible rests on computational functionalism — the claim that implementing the right computation is sufficient for consciousness — which is usually treated as obvious but is actually a contestable philosophical assumption.
Brains cannot be cleanly split into software and hardware

Unlike computers, where an algorithm is substrate-independent, a brain's biological materiality (metabolism, autopoiesis, multiscale dynamics) is inseparable from what it does, so there is no 'mindware' that could run equally well on silicon.
Being alive may be necessary for consciousness

Biological naturalism holds that the self-sustaining, metabolic, prediction-error-minimizing processes of living systems may be a necessary basis for conscious experience, not just an incidental substrate for computation.
Simulating a process is not the same as instantiating it

A computational simulation of X does not bring X into being unless X is itself an algorithmic process; a simulated rainstorm doesn't make anything wet, and a simulated brain wouldn't necessarily be conscious.
Actually-conscious and merely conscious-seeming AI pose different ethical risks

Whether or not machines are ever really conscious, systems that merely seem conscious already create distinct ethical dangers — from misplaced rights that hamper control, to psychological harm from treating feeling-seeming things as empty, or vice versa.
